findings.title: [P1] Reject NaN, Infinity, fractional, and unsafe timeout values
findings.body: `Number(value)` returns `NaN` for any non-numeric string, and `NaN <= 0` evaluates to `false`, so the validation passes and `NaN` is returned as a timeout (`src/options.ts:11-12`). The same hole admits `"Infinity"` and `"1e309"` (→ `Infinity`), `"1.5"` (→ 1.5), and `"9007199254740993"` (unsafe integer). The removed `!Number.isSafeInteger(timeout)` guard previously rejected every one of these with `"invalid timeout"`. A validation function whose entire purpose is to reject bad input now silently accepts it, and the poison values propagate: `NaN` defeats all downstream numeric comparisons, and Node's `setTimeout` coerces `NaN`/`Infinity` delays to 1 ms, making deadlines fire immediately instead of the configuration error surfacing. Restore a guard equivalent to `Number.isSafeInteger(timeout) && timeout > 0` (or `Number.isFinite` plus an integer check).

findings.title: [P2] Preserve base-10 parseInt semantics for accepted input forms
findings.body: `Number()` accepts and reinterprets string forms that `Number.parseInt(value, 10)` did not (`src/options.ts:11`): `"0x10"` now returns 16 (previously threw, since radix-10 parsing yields 0), `"1e3"` now returns 1000 (previously 1, because `parseInt` stopped at `e`), `"1.5"` now returns 1.5 (previously 1), and `"12ms"` now returns `NaN` (previously 12). Even after restoring a safe-integer guard, these interpretation changes remain and contradict the PR's stated goal of "preserving existing contracts". Either keep `Number.parseInt(value, 10)` for identical accepted-input semantics, or deliberately document the new accepted grammar (whole-string numeric, including exponent/hex forms).

findings.title: [P3] Add tests covering the changed parsing contract
findings.body: `parseTimeout` is exported but has no tests (and no current callers) in the repository, so the rewritten validation has no executable specification. A small table-driven test over `undefined`, valid positive integers, zero/negative, non-numeric strings, non-finite strings (`"Infinity"`, `"1e309"`), fractional, and prefix-garbage inputs (`"12ms"`) would have caught the P1 regression and would lock the intended contract for future changes.

All candidates are now validated against source. The changed lines are `src/options.ts:11-12` (RIGHT side); the function is exported with no other callers or tests in the repo. Merging the six lanes' overlapping candidates yields three confirmed findings: the dropped `Number.isSafeInteger` guard (reported by five lanes), the `Number` vs `parseInt` semantics change, and the missing test coverage.

# PR Review

**Verdict:** request_changes

## Overview
This PR rewrites timeout parsing in `src/options.ts`: `Number.parseInt(value, 10)` plus a `Number.isSafeInteger` guard is replaced by `Number(value)` with only a `timeout <= 0` check. The PR description claims to "refine behavior while preserving existing contracts."

The intent is plausible — `Number()` evaluates the whole string instead of silently accepting a numeric prefix — but the implementation breaks the function's core contract. The `<= 0` comparison cannot reject `NaN`, `Infinity`, fractional, or unsafe-integer results, so invalid inputs that previously threw are now returned as valid timeouts. A secondary semantics change (`Number` accepting hex/exponent/decimal forms that base-10 `parseInt` did not) also contradicts the stated "preserving existing contracts" goal.

## Verification
Verification was skipped: the discovery call (`action: list`) reported verification is disabled because no user-level `verificationBaselines` are configured, so no baseline was selected or run. Note that baseline execution runs PR code unsandboxed (filesystem/network) with supervision limited to the original POSIX process group; an external sandbox or container wrapper is recommended for untrusted PRs when verification is enabled.

## Findings

### [P1] Reject NaN, Infinity, fractional, and unsafe timeout values
**Severity:** P1
**Rationale:** `Number(value)` returns `NaN` for any non-numeric string, and `NaN <= 0` evaluates to `false`, so the validation passes and `NaN` is returned as a timeout (`src/options.ts:11-12`). The same hole admits `"Infinity"` and `"1e309"` (→ `Infinity`), `"1.5"` (→ 1.5), and `"9007199254740993"` (unsafe integer). The removed `!Number.isSafeInteger(timeout)` guard previously rejected every one of these with `"invalid timeout"`. A validation function whose entire purpose is to reject bad input now silently accepts it, and the poison values propagate: `NaN` defeats all downstream numeric comparisons, and Node's `setTimeout` coerces `NaN`/`Infinity` delays to 1 ms, making deadlines fire immediately instead of the configuration error surfacing. Restore a guard equivalent to `Number.isSafeInteger(timeout) && timeout > 0` (or `Number.isFinite` plus an integer check).
**Location:** `src/options.ts:11-12 RIGHT

### [P2] Preserve base-10 parseInt semantics for accepted input forms
**Severity:** P2
**Rationale:** `Number()` accepts and reinterprets string forms that `Number.parseInt(value, 10)` did not (`src/options.ts:11`): `"0x10"` now returns 16 (previously threw, since radix-10 parsing yields 0), `"1e3"` now returns 1000 (previously 1, because `parseInt` stopped at `e`), `"1.5"` now returns 1.5 (previously 1), and `"12ms"` now returns `NaN` (previously 12). Even after restoring a safe-integer guard, these interpretation changes remain and contradict the PR's stated goal of "preserving existing contracts". Either keep `Number.parseInt(value, 10)` for identical accepted-input semantics, or deliberately document the new accepted grammar (whole-string numeric, including exponent/hex forms).
**Location:** `src/options.ts:11 RIGHT`

### [P3] Add tests covering the changed parsing contract
**Severity:** P3
**Rationale:** `parseTimeout` is exported but has no tests (and no current callers) in the repository, so the rewritten validation has no executable specification. A small table-driven test over `undefined`, valid positive integers, zero/negative, non-numeric strings, non-finite strings (`"Infinity"`, `"1e309"`), fractional, and prefix-garbage inputs (`"12ms"`) would have caught the P1 regression and would lock the intended contract for future changes.
**Location:** `src/options.ts:11-12 RIGHT`

## Lane completeness
All requested lanes completed.

## Strengths and notes
- Preserves the existing `undefined` default of 5000 ms and the zero/negative rejection.
- Evaluating the full input string rather than a numeric prefix is a reasonable hardening goal — it is only the guard removal that makes it unsound.
- **Correctness:** invalid timeout strings now yield `NaN`/`Infinity`/fractional return values instead of throws (P1 above).
- **Security:** if timeout values originate from user/attacker-controlled configuration, non-finite values can effectively disable deadline enforcement instead of being rejected.
- **Performance:** `NaN`/`Infinity` delays are coerced by `setTimeout` to ~1 ms, which can turn retry or polling waits into tight loops.
